_readme: Famous asteroids for the Explorer. 'neo' is the NASA NeoWs id (orbit and close approaches are fetched live). 'approx' elements (a au, e, i/node/peri degrees) are rounded values from JPL's Small-Body Database, used only to draw the orbit when the live data can't be reached.

famous.name: 101955 Bennu
facts: NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought 121.6 g of Bennu back to Earth in September 2023.
An 'active asteroid': OSIRIS-REx saw it flinging small pebbles into space.

famous.name: 99942 Apophis
facts: On 13 April 2029 it will pass just 32,000 km above Earth — closer than geostationary satellites — and will be visible without a telescope.
NASA's OSIRIS-APEX will study it after the flyby. No chance of hitting Earth for at least 100 years.

famous.name: 65803 Didymos & Dimorphos
facts: NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into its moonlet Dimorphos in 2022 and shortened its orbit by 33 minutes — the first test of planetary defence.
ESA's Hera mission is on its way to inspect the crater.

famous.name: 162173 Ryugu
facts: Japan's Hayabusa2 returned 5.4 g of samples in 2020 — they contain amino acids.

famous.name: 433 Eros
facts: NASA's NEAR Shoemaker landed on it in 2001 — the first landing on an asteroid.

famous.name: 3200 Phaethon
facts: An 'active asteroid': it sheds dust when it swoops close to the Sun.
That dust makes the Geminid meteor shower every December.

famous.name: 25143 Itokawa
facts: Hayabusa brought back the first ever asteroid dust in 2010.

scheduled.name: 99942 Apophis (2029 flyby)
scheduled.note: Predicted, not this week: closest approach about 38,000 km from Earth's centre (about 32,000 km above the surface).
